 WATCH LIVE: Trump rallies in Iowa as part of final push before Election Day
 Politics 
 Nov 1, 2026 2:12 PM EST
 WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is closing out the final days of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he has handily won in the past while Democrats began to fracture in Michigan, risking their effort to retake the Senate.
 Trump's first stop is scheduled for Sunday afternoon in Dubuque, Iowa, where Republicans are battling to hold onto a critical Senate seat along with the governor's office. The 2nd Congressional District, which includes Dubuque, has also become competitive as the GOP works to protect its fragile majority in the House.
 Watch the Iowa rally in the video player above. 
 Trump plans to close out the last weekend of campaigning before Election Day on Tuesday with a visit to Salina, Kansas. Adam Hamilton is mounting a robust bid to become the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat in 94 years.
 With more than 52 million votes already cast, the trips reflect the GOP's defensive posture as the elections become a referendum on Trump's White House second term.

 They are a reminder of how starkly the political environment has changed since Trump's last campaign. In 2024, he worked to flip states that had previously backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. This year, Trump has focused largely on states he has dominated before as voters, including previous supporters, question the economic fallout of his decision to impose tariffs and launch the war in Iran.
 But Democrats who have become increasingly bullish on their prospects were confronting challenges of their own.
 In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's onetime opponent in the Senate primary, Haley Stevens, appeared with Republican Mike Rogers at a church service and later endorsed his campaign. Stevens, who has criticized El-Sayed as being insufficiently supportive of Israel, said she backed Rogers after an invitation to a Democratic event was rescinded.
 READ MORE: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses GOP's Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race 2 days before election 
 "Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."
 The stunning move forced other Democrats to reiterate their support for El-Sayed. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said the party was "united in our support." Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who leads the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said the party would "stand firmly" behind El-Sayed and "reject any efforts to divide Democrats."
 Earlier on Sunday, Sen. Bernie Sanders, a top supporter of El-Sayed, dismissed concerns about a Democratic divide.
 "Haley Stevens lost a very, very close primary. I can understand being upset about that," the Vermont independent said on CBS' "Face the Nation." "But from what I can see, all over the state, people are standing up, they're gonna stand with Abdul."
 Michigan plays a key role in the Democratic effort to retake control of the Senate. If they don't keep that seat on Tuesday, they would face additional pressure to win races in deeper Republican territory such as Texas, Kansas, Ohio or Iowa.
 Midterms test Trump's strength in GOP
 The campaign's closing stretch has largely become a test of Trump's enduring strength in a Republican Party he reshaped in his image a decade ago. He's hoping to energize voters like Jon Lutz, a Dubuque resident who watches videos of Trump all the time but is attending his first rally on Sunday.
 Lutz said he's happy with Trump's second term record and wants Republicans to keep control of the House and Senate so his agenda will advance.
 "He's done what he's said he's going to do," Lutz said. "I want him to keep going."
 For all the effort to reach Trump's supporters, the more than two dozen rallies he held in October were occasionally overshadowed by Trump's meandering asides and sometimes graphic descriptions of the physique of the male politicians he was supporting. Trump paused the rallies on Saturday and spent the evening at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida at a jungle-themed Halloween party, where he bragged about the wealth of his guests and dismissed concerns about the country's direction.
 "The country has never done better," he said.
 READ MORE: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses 
 Outgoing Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., raised concerns on Sunday that the president's policies, particularly tariffs, could weigh down the GOP.
 "Tariffs are not popular here in the Midwest," he told CNN's "State of the Union." "I tried telling the president that."
 Bacon predicted "there will be a debate in the party" about its future if there are significant losses this week.
 Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina was more optimistic. The chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee said he was confident Republicans would keep the Senate and embraced Trump's role in the campaign.
 "There's no doubt that President Trump has said himself that the midterm election is about him," he told NBC's "Meet the Press." "His agenda, without any question, is on the ballot."
 Associated Press writers Corey Williams in Detroit, Hannah Fingerhut in Dubuque, Iowa and Will Weissert and Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report.
